nodes.databaseMuscleNote: Seen in the recorded database fixture (server/fixtures/liveMuscleAggregation.ts: 'Rectus abdominis', muscle_group 'abdominals') and in shared/capabilityRank.ts; the database lane confirms.
nodes.location: Front of the abdomen, at the surface: one strap on each side of the midline, from the pubic bone up to the lower end of the breastbone and the cartilages of the fifth to seventh ribs.
nodes.whatItDoes: Bends your trunk forward, curling the ribs toward the pelvis, mostly through the lower back. It also helps press on the contents of the abdomen.
nodes.shapeNote: May contribute to the front contour of the abdomen. Tendinous bands divide it into segments that can show beneath the skin when body fat is low; the number of bands, and so of segments, differs between people. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: Drawn in segments, but it is one muscle: work is counted for the whole muscle.
Studies disagree on whether exercises can work its upper and lower parts differently.
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: A surface muscle at the front of the abdomen (kenhub.rectus_abdominis, imaios.rectus_abdominis); Kenhub says it is clearly visible beneath the skin in people with low body fat. Body fat hides it in many people, as for every surface muscle; the shape note says so. 'variable' would also be defensible if the lane reads visibility as dependent on body fat.
nodes.layerCheck: §1.2 'surface': supported (Kenhub: on the anterior surface of the abdominal wall). It lies inside the rectus sheath, whose front wall is the tendon sheets of the side muscles (imaios.rectus_abdominis), and the small pyramidalis lies in front of its lowest part (elsevier.rectus_abdominis); neither is a muscle belly over it, so 'surface' holds. §1.2's 'one node (drawn in segments)' matches the anatomy: the tendinous intersections divide one muscle.

nodes.name: External oblique
nodes.databaseMuscleNote: Seen in the recorded database fixture (server/fixtures/liveMuscleAggregation.ts: 'External oblique', muscle_group 'obliques') and in shared/capabilityRank.ts.
nodes.location: Side and front of the abdomen, at the surface: from the outer faces of the lower eight ribs to the crest of the hip bone, the pubic bone and the midline band.
nodes.whatItDoes: With both sides working, bends your trunk forward and presses on the abdomen. With one side working, bends the trunk to that side and turns it toward the other side.
nodes.shapeNote: May contribute to the contour of the side of the waist and, where its slips interlock with the serratus anterior, of the lower ribs at the side of the chest. caveats: Twisting work loads it together with the internal oblique of the other side, which turns the trunk the same way; this page does not split that work between them.
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: The most superficial of the flat muscles (kenhub.external_abdominal_oblique, teachmeanatomy.abdominal_wall, imaios.external_abdominal_oblique), but only its side part is muscle: toward the front it becomes an aponeurosis that covers the rectus abdominis (kenhub.external_abdominal_oblique). 'partial' is an inference from that.
nodes.layerCheck: §1.2 'surface': supported by three references. For the drawing lane: its belly is at the side; the part in front of the rectus abdominis is tendon sheet, drawn as structure or not at all.

nodes.name: Internal oblique
nodes.databaseMuscleNote: Listed in shared/capabilityRank.ts (internal_oblique: 'obliques'); not seen in the recorded database fixture. The database lane checks it.
nodes.location: Side of the abdomen, middle layer: under the external oblique and over the transversus abdominis, between the lower ribs and the top of the hip bone.
nodes.whatItDoes: With both sides working, bends your trunk forward and presses on the abdomen. With one side working, bends the trunk to that side and turns it toward the same side. It also helps you breathe out hard.
nodes.shapeNote: Lies under the external oblique, so it has little separately visible contour; it may add to the general thickness of the side of the waist. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: Twisting work loads it together with the external oblique of the other side, which turns the trunk the same way; this page does not split that work between them.
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: Covered by the external oblique at the front and side (teachmeanatomy.abdominal_wall, statpearls.anterolateral_abdominal_wall, kenhub.external_abdominal_oblique). nodes.layerCheck: §1.2 'intermediate', no outcrop: supported (the middle of the three flat muscles in StatPearls' layer order, under the external oblique in TeachMeAnatomy and Kenhub). The inferior lumbar triangle at the back of the waist is the one place no muscle covers it (Radiopaedia); the core's drawing has a front view only (§7.2), so no outcrop is needed. Not a deviation.

nodes.name: Transversus abdominis
nodes.databaseMuscleNote: Listed in shared/capabilityRank.ts (transversus_abdominis: 'abdominals'); not seen in the recorded database fixture. The database lane checks it.
nodes.location: Abdominal wall, deepest layer: wraps around the abdomen from the cartilages of the lower ribs, the fascia of the lower back and the hip bone to the midline band at the front.

nodes.shapeNote: The deepest layer of the abdominal wall, under both obliques, so it has little or no contour of its own. Visible shape depends on the muscles over it, body fat and individual anatomy.

sources.title: Kenhub: Rectus abdominis: Origin, insertion, innervation, function
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q5, Q42, Q49, Kenhub only). Function: trunk flexion, compression of the abdominal viscera, and expiration (Q5, tied to 'Kenhub's muscle page'). Location: a paired muscle running vertically either side of the linea alba on the front of the abdominal wall, from the pubic crest and symphysis to the xiphoid process and the cartilages of ribs 5-7; three tendinous intersections, at the xiphoid, the umbilicus and midway, sometimes four; 'In those with low body fat, it is clearly visible beneath the skin forming the six pack'. sources.title: Sarti MA, Monfort M, Fuster MA, Villaplana LA. Muscle activity in upper and lower rectus abdominus during abdominal exercises. Arch Phys Med Rehabil 1996;77(12):1293-7
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q30, Q32): PubMed abstract. Nonrandomized trial, convenience sample of 33 healthy volunteers split by activity level and by whether they performed the exercises correctly; surface EMG (average iEMG) of the upper and lower rectus abdominis in curl-ups and posterior pelvic tilts. Correct performers: curl-ups gave greater upper-part activity in both activity groups; the pelvic tilt worked the lower part harder than the curl-up only in the high-activity correct-performer subgroup; incorrect performers activated both parts about equally. sources.title: Clark, Holt, Sinyard. Electromyographic comparison of the upper and lower rectus abdominis during abdominal exercises. J Strength Cond Res 2003;17(3):475-83
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q30, Q33): PubMed abstract of a pilot study; eight healthy adults, six abdominal exercises in random order (including the curl-up, a curl-up on an exercise ball and leg lowering); no significant difference between upper and lower rectus abdominis EMG in any exercise. The search did not show the author list (the query named Clark, Holt and Sinyard; not confirmed). Abstract only. Second review (R7): the journal's abstract page (journals.lww.com) and PubMed 12930172 were returned; the summary names the authors Clark, Holt and Sinyard (initials not shown), calls it a pilot study and gives the same result: no significant difference between the upper and lower rectus abdominis in any exercise. Activity did differ between exercises (the curl-up variants higher than the reverse curl-up, leg lowering and a ball roll-out). Two of the six exercises are named by brand in the abstract; copy does not name them.

sources.title: Escamilla RF, Babb E, DeWitt R, et al. Electromyographic analysis of traditional and nontraditional abdominal exercises: implications for rehabilitation and training. Phys Ther 2006;86(5):656-71
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q28, Q31, Q46). The abstract was seen through a search summary beside a Sacramento State repository record (scholars.csus.edu): surface EMG of 21 healthy adults aged 23-43, normalised to maximum voluntary contractions, from the upper and lower rectus abdominis, external and internal obliques, rectus femoris, latissimus dorsi and lumbar paraspinals; upper and lower rectus abdominis, internal oblique and latissimus dorsi activity highest in roll-outs, pikes and knee-ups on a wheeled device, hanging knee-ups with straps and reverse crunches on a 30-degree incline; external oblique highest in the wheeled-device exercises and hanging knee-ups with straps; the same exercises most effective at activating extraneous muscles; lumbar paraspinal activity low and similar across exercises. The full list of exercises compared was not shown. The PMID 16649890 and the author list come from secondary citations (two blog posts and a magazine article), not from PubMed; the DOI was given by one of them and by the summary. Not to be confused with the same first author's 2006 JOSPT paper on commercial devices (PubMed 16494072). The wheeled device is named by its brand in the abstract; athlete copy does not name it. Second review (R8, R19): PubMed 16649890 was returned under this title, so the PMID is now seen on PubMed (the first review had it from secondary citations) and the URL points there; the Oxford Academic abstract page (academic.oup.com/ptj/article-abstract/86/5/656/2857416) was also returned. The abstract lines agree: 21 healthy men and women aged 23-43; the highest activity as cited; lumbar paraspinal activity low and similar; the authors' conclusion that the same exercises were also the most effective in activating extraneous musculature; rectus femoris highest in the wheeled-device pike and knee-up, the inclined reverse crunch and the bent-knee sit-up. The author list beyond Escamilla is still from secondary citations. One summary attributed the abstract to JOSPT 36(2), which is the same first author's other 2006 paper (PubMed 16494072); the lines quoted match the Physical Therapy paper.

sources.title: Snarr RL, Esco MR. Electromyographical comparison of plank variations performed with and without instability devices. J Strength Cond Res 2014;28(11):3298-3305
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q38, Q39): abstract seen through a summary beside the BISp sports-literature record and university repository listings. Twelve healthy adults (six men, six women), isometric holds of five plank variations in random order; EMG of the rectus abdominis, external oblique and erector spinae; planks on instability devices produced higher activity in these surface muscles than the stable plank; the authors advise caution for people with lower-back weakness because erector spinae activity rose. The devices themselves were not named in the abstract excerpt (a 2017 write-up the summary linked to the study mentions an exercise ball and a suspension device; not used). PMID not seen. Second review (R10, R13): re-keyed from bisp.plank_instability_emg to lww.plank_instability_emg, since BISp is a sports-literature database, not the publisher, and the key form is <publisher>.<topic>; the journal's own page at journals.lww.com was returned and the URL now points there (the BISp record, www.bisp-surf.de/Record/PU201501000974, is where the first review saw the abstract). The summary confirms the authors, journal, pages and DOI, twelve healthy men and women, and the result that planks with instability devices increased EMG of the superficial musculature compared with stable planks. Results for each muscle and each device were not shown in either review; a later paper (R10) cites it for higher activation with an exercise ball and a suspension device. No PubMed entry was returned.

sources.title: Urquhart DM, Hodges PW. Differential activity of regions of transversus abdominis during trunk rotation. Eur Spine J 2005;14(4):393-400
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q35, Q45): abstract on Springer Medicine and the University of Queensland's publication listing. Six people with no history of spinal pain; fine-wire electrodes in the upper, middle and lower transversus abdominis and in the obliques, surface electrodes over the rectus abdominis; seated trunk rotation in both directions. The transversus abdominis was active throughout rotation, its upper fibres recruited in the opposite pattern to its middle and lower fibres; the rectus abdominis showed no directional difference. A later commentary in the same results reads it as activity in both directions, stronger when the chest turns toward the muscle's side, and notes the muscle's small moment arm for rotation. PMID not seen. Second review (R4, R12): PubMed 15940481 was returned for this title, so the source is now keyed by its PMID (it was springer.transversus_rotation_emg; the Springer Medicine page, www.springermedicine.com/differential-activity-of-regions-of-transversus-abdominis-during/21220578, is where the first review saw the abstract). The PubMed abstract says rotation was done 'in sitting by rotating the pelvis relative to a fixed thorax', that the transversus abdominis 'was consistently active during trunk rotation, with the recruitment patterns of the upper fascicles opposite to that of the middle and lower fascicles', and that the fine-wire electrodes were in one side of the abdominal wall. The snippet stopped before the rectus abdominis result, which rests on the first review's excerpt (Q35).

sources.title: Tayashiki K, Takai Y, Maeo S, Kanehisa H. Intra-abdominal Pressure and Trunk Muscular Activities during Abdominal Bracing and Hollowing. Int J Sports Med 2016;37(2):134-143
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q26, Q44): abstract on Thieme Connect. Seven young adult men; pressure inside the abdomen measured with a rectal transducer, with surface EMG of the rectus abdominis, external oblique, internal oblique and erector spinae. The rise in pressure was far greater in bracing than in hollowing; at peak pressure activity was higher in bracing than hollowing and higher in the internal oblique than in the other three muscles; pressure and muscle activity were linearly related in both tasks, with a task-specific relationship. The transversus abdominis was not recorded. Abstract only; PMID not seen. Second review (R11): PubMed 26509386 and the Thieme abstract page were returned; now keyed by the PMID (it was thieme.bracing_hollowing_iap; the Thieme page, thieme-connect.de/products/ejournals/html/10.1055/s-0035-1559771, is where the first review saw the abstract). The summary agrees with every line cited: seven young adult men, a rectal pressure transducer, surface EMG of the four muscles, a rise of 116.4 against 9.9 mmHg, higher activity in bracing and in the internal oblique at peak pressure, and a task-specific linear relation.

sources.title: Tuominen et al. The prevalence and consequences of abdominal rectus muscle diastasis among Finnish women: an epidemiological cohort study. Hernia 2022;26:599-608
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q41, Q48): abstract (PMC, Springer and Springer Medicine copies). Prospective cohort at Helsinki University Hospital; linea alba width measured by ultrasound at the early pregnancy scan in 933 women; mean width about 1.81 cm in women with no earlier pregnancy, about 2.36 cm after one and 2.55 cm after more, rising with the number of earlier pregnancies; severe diastasis (over 5 cm) rare; moderate diastasis not explaining back pain or disability at the population level. Second review (R15): the Springer and PMC pages were returned; the summary names the first author, Tuominen, and places the paper in Hernia 26:599-608 (2022; published online 2021, DOI 10.1007/s10029-021-02484-8). It repeats the methods and results cited and adds that symptoms were measured with the Oswestry Disability Index and RAND-36. The other authors were not shown.

disagreements: Transversus abdominis and turning the trunk: Kenhub lists ipsilateral rotation on one-sided contraction; Radiopaedia, IMAIOS and Elsevier list compression only (Q10, Q11, Q21). The function claim states the disagreement; no spine.rotation node action is recorded. The fine-wire study (pmid.15940481) shows it active during turning, which is activity, not torque; a commentary in the same results calls its moment arm for rotation small.

External oblique, side of lateral flexion: Kenhub (and anatomy.app, not cited) say the same side; LearnMuscles (not cited) gives no side; Elsevier says 'laterally flexes' with no side. The claim says 'to that side', the anatomical reading of Kenhub's 'ipsilateral'.

Rectus abdominis and side bending: one unidentified physiotherapy source (Q15) and an IMAIOS veterinary entry say it helps bend the trunk sideways; no human anatomy reference cited here lists it. Not claimed; no spine.lateral_flexion node action.
Rectus abdominis and tilting the pelvis back: mentioned by an untied line in Q1 and by LearnMuscles for the group (Q7); not confirmed by Kenhub (Q5). Not claimed (not a region action either).

Upper versus lower rectus abdominis: Sarti 1996 found differences in correct performers; the 2003 pilot found none; a later paper groups Lehman and McGill 2001 with the studies finding none (Q29, abstract not seen, not cited). The selectivity claim says the question is unsettled.

Number of tendinous intersections: three in most references; three to four (IMAIOS, a Kenhub video); one to five in two cadaver series. The appearance claim says 'usually three'; the variation claim gives the range.

Pressure in the abdomen as a spine stabiliser: contested (Q27: a review argues the proposed mechanism lacks experimental support; a thesis says it cannot be determined with certainty). Kenhub's line that the abdominal muscles 'stabilize the vertebral column' with the back muscles is not used. No claim says that bracing steadies the spine.
Rectus abdominis and compression, prime or assist: MeSH (Gray's) says it 'assists'; Kenhub, IMAIOS and Elsevier list compression unqualified. Recorded as assist (see nodeActions).

External oblique, attachment to the hip bone (second review): Kenhub's excerpt has the tendon sheet reach the front of the iliac crest; Radiopaedia has the lowest fibres attach there as muscle and the tendon sheet go to the midline band and the pubic bone (R2). The appearance claim now says only that its lowest fibres reach the crest, which both support.

Transversus abdominis and breathing out (second review): StatPearls' abdominal wall chapter (R22, not cited) says the side muscles except the transversus abdominis help breathe out by pulling the ribs down; Kenhub and IMAIOS say it aids forced expiration, Kenhub through its compression. The function claim now says it helps 'through that compression', which no source contradicts. The same search returned StatPearls' chapter on the wall's muscles saying the flat muscles, as a group, flex and rotate the trunk; it does not single out the transversus abdominis, so the claim's 'the others' (the cited Radiopaedia, IMAIOS and Elsevier pages, which list no trunk movement for it) stands.

Upper versus lower rectus abdominis (second review): two further studies, not cited, keep the question open: a 2023 ultrasound-thickness study of 15 people whose authors say 'controversy exists' (R5, PubMed 38288259), and a study of exercises on and off an exercise ball that found more upper than lower activity in curl-ups (R6). The selectivity claim now opens 'Studies disagree' rather than 'is unsettled'.

The obliques in forward bending, prime or assist (second review): Kenhub has them flex the trunk together with the rectus abdominis (R18); no reference returned grades them. Recorded as prime, as the first review did; open for the anatomy lane.
notes.abdomenCompression: What the evidence supports about abdomen.compression (bracing, raising pressure in the abdomen): every anatomy reference cited lists compressing the abdomen as an action of the three flat muscles; for the transversus abdominis it is the main and, in three of four references, the only action, with raising intra-abdominal pressure named by Radiopaedia, Kenhub and IMAIOS; the internal oblique (five references) and the external oblique (Kenhub, Elsevier) compress the abdomen when both sides act; the rectus abdominis 'assists' (MeSH) or compresses (Kenhub, IMAIOS, Elsevier). One measured study (pmid.26509386, seven men, abstract only) found that bracing raised the pressure far more than drawing the belly in, that pressure and muscle activity rose together, and that the internal oblique was the most active of the four trunk muscles recorded; the transversus abdominis was not recorded. Not supported here, so not claimed: that raised pressure steadies the spine (contested, Q27); that the diaphragm and pelvic floor share the work (seen only in a thesis and a blog, Q27); any figure for how much each muscle contributes (the 1992 intramuscular study, Q22 and Q24, was seen only as a reference-list entry). Node actions: transversus abdominis, internal oblique and external oblique prime; rectus abdominis assist. Second review: independent results agree. TeachMeAnatomy (R1) says the rectus abdominis 'assists the flat muscles in compressing the abdominal viscera', which supports assist rather than prime for it. StatPearls (R21, R22) says the wall takes part in any activity that raises the pressure inside the abdomen and that the abdominal muscles contracting together raise it in coughing, sneezing and vomiting. Tayashiki et al. (pmid.26509386) is confirmed (R11). Intramuscular studies by Cresswell and colleagues (R16: 1992, six men; 1994, lifting) were seen only as partial abstracts: in the 1994 study the transversus abdominis had the highest activity of the abdominal muscles and the best correlation with the pressure. They are consistent with its prime role but are not cited until an abstract is tied. Nothing found says how much each muscle contributes in bracing, and nothing here says that bracing steadies the spine.

The transversus abdominis's early activation before arm and leg movements, and its timing in people with low back pain: a known clinical literature, not searched as a selectivity claim (it is not about which exercise loads which muscle); results in Q45 also show it is disputed.

Plank and side-plank variations beyond the one tied abstract: the long-lever posterior-tilt plank (Q37), side-bridge variants (Q36, Q50) and suspended planks (Q39) were found only as citations or untied summaries. Second review: tied abstracts were found for the long-lever, posterior-tilt plank (R24, R26: Schoenfeld and colleagues, Sports Biomechanics 2014, 19 participants) and for the side bridge (R27: Ekstrom, Donatelli and Carp, JOSPT 2007, PubMed 18560185); listed as candidate claims in secondReview.candidateClaims, not added.

Anti-rotation work (a press held against a sideways pull): the only EMG study found (Q39) is a small methodology study in a conference-abstract series; not cited. Second review (R20): no study measuring a press held against a sideways pull was returned either.
The 1998 intramuscular study of psoas and the abdominal wall across many tasks (Q34): abstract not seen.
Any statement that a muscle grows, or how much an exercise loads it: no claim says either.
